sources.title: Book request #184: 'Nix from First Principles' syllabus and editorial principles
Dolstra, The Purely Functional Software Deployment Model (2006)
Software Sustainability Institute: Reproducible Environments With Nix
Home Manager docs: Nix Flakes (mirror of nix-flakes.adoc)
DEV Community: overview of Nix, NixOS, Nixpkgs
Examples run locally with Nix 2.34.6 (nix-instantiate --eval, nix repl)
Hands-on runs of raw derivations with Nix 2.34.6 (nix-instantiate, nix-store --realise, nix derivation show)

structure.rationale: The order follows the requester's syllabus and its central question — how a description becomes a package, a dev environment, or a system. It goes: motivation and map, the store, the language, derivations and the build lifecycle, packaging and customization, dev environments and flakes, real applications and CI, then modules, Home Manager and NixOS (kept optional until late), and finally debugging, a capstone and contributing. Each chapter keeps the requester's seven-beat rhythm. Note: web fetches (nix.dev, Nix manual) were refused by the proxy during scaffolding, so no external sources were consulted yet; each concept page must fetch and record its sources before writing.
structure.audience: Developers comfortable with a terminal, git, one programming language and basic build/dependency workflows; no prior Nix or NixOS knowledge.

claims.text: Conventional package managers install into shared global locations (e.g. /usr/lib), so two programs needing different versions of one library compete for the same path; this is the 'dependency hell' Nix was designed to avoid.
Nix stores each package under a path containing a hash of all its inputs, so versions coexist side by side and upgrades/rollbacks are atomic.

Builds and install scripts often depend on undeclared things on the host (tools on PATH, system libraries, env vars, locale, OS version); these hidden assumptions are the usual cause of 'works on my machine'.

Recording what is installed (a snapshot such as pip freeze or a package list) lists results, not the inputs and steps that produced them, and usually omits the OS-level tools and libraries; a description states what should be present and how it is made.
Language lock files (mix.lock, Cargo.lock) pin language libraries but not the compiler, OS libraries or tools outside the language's package manager.
Nix builds run in a sandbox (default on Linux, not default on macOS) so undeclared dependencies fail loudly instead of silently working.

snippets.code: mix deps.get && mix phx.server   # assumes: Elixir, Erlang/OTP, a C compiler, Postgres client libs, inotify-tools already exist
snippets.note: illustrative hidden-assumption example for the book's Phoenix project; no Nix syntax in this chapter

pitfalls: Do not claim Nix makes everything perfectly reproducible; later chapters cover where it breaks down.
Do not show Nix syntax here; the chapter is motivation only.
Lock files help but only cover one layer.

claims.text: The word 'Nix' names several things: a purely functional language for describing builds, the package manager/build tool that evaluates it, and the culture around them; NixOS configuration is written in the same language.
The Nix package manager runs on Linux and other Unix-like systems (including macOS); NixOS is a full Linux distribution built on top of it, so NixOS is optional for using Nix.
Nixpkgs is the package collection: a very large set of package definitions, each written as a derivation-producing expression in the Nix language.
NixOS describes a whole operating system declaratively; configurations can be version-controlled and rolled back.
Home Manager manages user-level packages and dotfiles with Nix; it can run standalone (the only option on non-NixOS, non-nix-darwin systems) or as a module inside a NixOS or nix-darwin configuration.

Flakes are a project-level interface: a directory with flake.nix declaring inputs and outputs, with flake.lock pinning exact input revisions. They need the nix-command and flakes experimental features enabled and the docs still describe them as experimental.
Flakes were introduced with Nix 2.4.
Nix builds in a sandbox by default on Linux, which is why the store-and-derivation model is trusted for reproducibility.

snippets.note: illustrative; nix run needs nix-command and flakes enabled; first-run detail covered in chapter 3

pitfalls: 'Nix' is used for the language, the tool and loosely the whole ecosystem; always say which.
NixOS is not required to use Nix, Nixpkgs or Home Manager.
Do not treat flakes as a separate package manager; they are an interface over the same evaluation and build.
Mentioned names (nix-darwin, Cachix) are only pointers here; details come later.

claims.text: The recommended install on Linux and macOS is multi-user mode (a Nix daemon runs builds); the install command is: curl -L https://nixos.org/nix/install | sh -s -- --daemon.
Multi-user mode on Linux needs systemd with SELinux disabled; otherwise single-user install is the fallback. macOS is supported.
With the daemon, store-changing actions by an unprivileged user are forwarded to the Nix daemon.
Some macOS 15 Sequoia upgrades broke installs with a missing _nixbld group/user error (NixOS/nix issue #10892).
The installer accepts --help to list flags.
The `nix` command (nix run, nix shell, nix build, nix develop) needs nix-command (and for nixpkgs# references, flakes) experimental features enabled unless the installer enabled them.

`nix run nixpkgs#hello` fetches/builds the program into the store and runs it without adding it to your profile or PATH; `nix shell nixpkgs#cowsay` gives a subshell with the tool on PATH that disappears on exit.
`nix build` leaves a `result` symlink in the current directory pointing into /nix/store; it is a link, not a copy.
`nix develop` enters a development shell for a flake/derivation; `nix-shell -p` is the older equivalent for ad-hoc environments.

snippets.note: install command per nix.dev; version output varies
illustrative; one-off enabling; permanent: experimental-features = nix-command flakes in nix.conf (unsourced)

snippets.code:
nix shell nixpkgs#cowsay nixpkgs#lolcat
nix build nixpkgs#hello && ls -l result && ./result/bin/hello
snippets.note: unsourced, widely documented behaviour; the book tells the reader to check for themselves

pitfalls: Web fetches were refused by the proxy; several claims have no source and the page tells readers to verify by running.
Piping a script to sh: advise reading it first.
Flakes/nix-command wording is experimental; do not state stability firmly.
Exact output/store hashes differ per machine; do not print fake hashes as real.
Do not explain the store in depth; next chapter.

claims.text: A store path is the store directory (default /nix/store), a slash, a 32-character digest, a hyphen, and a human-readable name; the digest is the first 160 bits of a SHA-256 hash of a fingerprint, written in a custom base-32 alphabet.
The base-32 alphabet uses digits and lowercase letters except e, o, u and t.

A store path refers to exactly one store object. For ordinary builds the digest is derived from the build description (its inputs), not from the output bytes; content-addressed paths are named from their contents.
Because the digest covers all inputs, different versions or different build options of the same package get different paths and coexist side by side.

Nix finds an output's runtime dependencies by scanning it for the hash parts of its build inputs' store paths; any match becomes a reference. References can be created accidentally (e.g. a compiler path left in an rpath).

nix-store --query --references prints a path's immediate dependencies; --requisites prints its whole closure; nix path-info -r walks the closure recursively and can show sizes (-s) and closure sizes (-S).
The garbage collector deletes store paths not used, directly or indirectly, by any generation of any profile or any other root.
GC roots are registered as symlinks, e.g. under /nix/var/nix/gcroots; profiles and their generations are roots; the result link from nix build is an indirect root registered under gcroots/auto.
nix-collect-garbage -d deletes old generations of profiles (current user unless run as root) and then collects, which makes rollback to those generations impossible.

A profile is a symlink to an immutable set of installed packages; each change makes a new numbered generation, and old ones stay until deleted. On common setups the user profile is reached via ~/.nix-profile and /nix/var/nix/profiles/.
Store contents are readable by every user on the machine, so secrets must not be put in the store (developed in a later chapter).

snippets.code:
nix build nixpkgs#hello
readlink result
nix path-info -rsSh nixpkgs#hello
nix-store --query --references $(readlink -f result)
snippets.note: commands per the manual; output (hashes, sizes) differs per machine and is not printed in the page

pitfalls: Do not print invented hashes as if real; use a placeholder like <hash>.
Installing vs building: building puts a path in the store; installing adds it to a profile (a new generation).
Deleting the result link makes the build collectable, it does not delete it immediately.
nix-collect-garbage -d removes rollback points.
The path hash is of the inputs for ordinary builds, not of the output bytes.

claims.text: Strings are written in double quotes; ${ } embeds another expression; indented multi-line strings use two single quotes.
A path literal needs at least one slash (./builder.sh); without one, builder.sh parses as an attribute selection from variable builder. Interpolation works inside paths.
An attribute set is a collection of name-value pairs; attribute names may be interpolated, e.g. { ${bar} = 123; }.foo.
The // operator merges two attribute sets; on a clashing name the right-hand side wins (example: add // { x = 1; }).
Nix is a pure, functional language where a file holds a single expression that evaluates to a value; there are no statements and bindings are not reassigned.
let a = 1; in expr binds local names visible only inside expr; if/then/else is an expression and must have an else branch; lists are space-separated, not comma-separated; ++ concatenates lists.
Selecting a missing attribute is an error unless a default is given with `or`: set.x or 0. `rec` lets attributes in a set refer to each other; `inherit x;` copies a name in scope into a set.

snippets.note: Evaluate with nix eval --file project.nix (or nix-instantiate --eval --strict project.nix). Result: label "hello-2.12", settings.debug true, tools four names, mode "user".

pitfalls: Lists use spaces; commas silently make wrong lists or errors.
Every binding ends with a semicolon, including the last.
Nix is not shell: a file is one expression, not a list of commands run in order.
A path without a slash is a variable name, not a path.
// is shallow: nested sets are replaced, not merged.
Interpolating a path into a string copies it into the store.

claims.text: Every Nix function takes exactly one argument; several arguments are written as nested functions (currying), so passing one argument returns a function that can be reused.
A function can destructure an attribute-set argument, e.g. { name, age ? 42 }: ...; fields with a default (?) may be omitted by the caller.
An ellipsis (...) in the pattern lets the function accept sets with more attributes than it names; without it, extra attributes are an error.
The @ pattern binds the whole argument set to a name; defaulted arguments the caller omitted are NOT included in that bound set, so reading them from it fails.
Function application is by juxtaposition with a space (f x), binds tighter than operators, and is left-associative.
Scope is lexical: a function sees the names visible where it was written, not where it is called.

import path reads a .nix file and returns the value of its single expression; if that value is a function, import ./f.nix { ... } calls it. Splitting a project across files is just import plus function calls.
map f list applies f to each element (builtins.map, also in scope as map); functions are ordinary values and can be passed and returned.
The { pkgs, ... }: ... header is the same attribute-set-with-ellipsis pattern; Nixpkgs' callPackage fills in such arguments by name from a package set (covered later in the book).

snippets.note: one file = one function; reasoned from the language rules, not run in this session

snippets.code: let x = 1; f = y: x + y; in let x = 100; in f 1

pitfalls: Writing f(x) or f, x: is not Nix; arguments are separated by spaces and each function takes one.
Without ... a set with extra attributes is rejected.
With name@{ a ? 1 }, the omitted default is missing from name.
A function is not a value you can print; nix eval on one errors.
Passing 2 args to a one-set function: use one set, not two args.
import of a path without ./ is a variable lookup (see chapter 5).
functions-scope-and-composition.volatile_note: Page examples were reasoned from language rules; the nix manual fetch was refused by the proxy, so only nix-1p was consulted.

claims.text: Attribute values are evaluated only when selected: { a = 1; b = throw "boom"; }.a gives 1, but asking for the whole set with --strict (forcing every value) raises 'boom'.
List elements are lazy: builtins.length [ 1 (throw "x") 3 ] gives 3. Function arguments are lazy: (a: 5) (abort "never") gives 5.

rec { a = b + 1; b = a + 1; }.a fails with 'error: infinite recursion encountered', and the trace names the attribute being evaluated. rec { a = 1; b = a + 1; } is fine (b = 2): rec alone is not the problem, a value that needs itself is.
let xs = [1 2 3] ++ xs; in builtins.length xs is also 'infinite recursion encountered'.

Lazy self-reference works when the self-reference sits in a part nobody forces: nat = n: { head = n; tail = nat (n + 1); } is an endless stream; a take function over it returns [ 0 1 2 3 ] for take 4.

builtins.seq a b forces a to weak head normal form (only the outer layer of a set/list) then returns b; builtins.deepSeq forces everything inside. seq { a = throw "shallow"; } 1 gives 1, deepSeq of the same throws.
builtins.trace msg value prints 'trace: msg' to stderr and returns value; it is evaluated only when the surrounding expression is forced.
builtins.tryEval (throw "x") returns { success = false; value = false; }; tryEval catches throw and assert failures but not abort, and only forces to weak head normal form.

Evaluation errors (missing attribute, 'cannot add a string to an integer', undefined variable, missing function argument, throw, infinite recursion) happen before any build starts; build errors come from a builder running later. Errors print a chain of '… while evaluating the attribute' lines; --show-trace gives the full, untruncated trace.
'n-1' without spaces is parsed as one identifier, giving "undefined variable 'n-1'"; write n - 1.

In nix repl, ':l file.nix' loads a file's attributes into scope ('Added 4 variables'); evaluating a name shows its value, ':t' shows its type ('an integer'), ':p' prints a value fully forced; ':r' reloads. A rec set with a bad attribute loads fine and fails only when that attribute is evaluated.
Because import is just a function call, importing a file whose expression is a set with unused throwing attributes costs nothing for those attributes: v.ok works while v.never would throw.
Nixpkgs relies on laziness: it is one huge attribute set of packages, and only the packages you select are evaluated.

snippets.code: let x = { a = 1; b = throw "boom"; }; in x.a

pitfalls: Beginners read rec as the cause of infinite recursion; the cause is a value that depends on itself.
Printing a set in the REPL/eval may show nothing wrong until --strict or :p forces a bad value; laziness moves the error to where the value is used.
n-1 is one name; write n - 1.
seq only forces the outer layer; use deepSeq to hunt hidden errors, never leave it in real code.
tryEval does not catch abort or errors inside nested values.

claims.text: builtins.derivation takes an attribute set; name, system and builder are required. Evaluating it yields an attribute set of type "derivation" (type = "derivation") carrying drvPath, outPath and the outputs; it is a description, nothing is built yet.
nix-instantiate on a file whose value is a derivation writes a .drv file into the store and prints its path; nothing is built. nix-store --realise <drv> runs the builder and prints the output path.

Every attribute besides the reserved ones becomes an environment variable for the builder (strings as-is; paths copied into the store and passed as store paths). Nix also sets out (the output path), name, system and builder in env; args become the builder's command-line arguments.

The builder runs in a sandbox with a nearly empty filesystem: with builder = "/bin/sh" only the shell is available; /bin/cat and /usr/bin/tr gave 'not found' (exit code 127). Shell builtins like read and echo work. Real builds use store paths of tools (e.g. ${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/cat).
The builder must create the file or directory at $out; it is the only place it should write. Output path is computed before building, from the .drv's content.

Changing any input (an env attribute value, args, builder, or an upstream derivation) changes the .drv path and the output path: appending '!' to a greeting string produced a new .drv and a new output, while the old pair stayed in the store.
nix derivation show <drv> prints JSON with args, builder, env, inputs {drvs, srcs}, name, outputs (out path) and system (format version 4 in Nix 2.34). Older nix show-derivation is the same idea.

Interpolating one derivation into another's string ("${note}") yields its output store path and makes the first a dependency: the second .drv lists the first under inputs.drvs, and nix-store -q --references <drv> shows the input .drv. The dependency is on the .drv; building the second builds the first.

A build-time dependency is not automatically a runtime dependency: the output of a builder that merely read the note's file did not contain the note's store path, so nix-store -q --references of that output was empty. Runtime references come from store paths found inside the output.
Interpolating a local path such as "${./f.txt}" copies the file into the store and gives a store path (e.g. /nix/store/…-f.txt); changing the file's contents changes the path.

snippets.note: verified Nix 2.34.6 x86_64-linux; instantiates to a .drv, builds to a file containing the greeting
verified: output file contains 'hello, world'; shout.drv lists note.drv as an input drv

snippets.code:
nix-instantiate hello.nix
nix derivation show /nix/store/…-hello-note.drv
nix-store --realise /nix/store/…-hello-note.drv
nix-store -q --references /nix/store/…-shout.drv

pitfalls: A raw builder sees no cat, tr, grep or coreutils: only /bin/sh and its builtins, so 'not found' / exit code 127.
Forgetting to create $out gives a build error ('builder failed to produce output path').
Edit the file and the .drv name changes completely: that is the feature, not a bug.
A path to a store file in a string is a dependency only if Nix sees it as a string context; writing a store path by hand does not.
nix-instantiate warns about --add-root: the .drv may be garbage-collected.
